abstract: Horizontal gene transfer mediated by conjugative plasmids is a primary driver of bacterial evolution and the spread of adaptive traits, including antibiotic resistance determinants. Tracking how these plasmids disseminate through complex microbial communities remains a major challenge. Current methodologies often yield static, endpoint snapshots of host identity, overlooking transient transfer events and plasmid encounters with the co-resident mobilome. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SPacer Integration (SPI) plasmids, which turn the mobile element itself into a recorder of its own transfer history. We engineered conjugative and mobilizable plasmids to carry a CRISPR-Cas adaptation cassette (cas1-cas2 and a minimal CRISPR array) and maintain tight repression of cas1-cas2 expression in the donor cell, so that upon transfer they capture spacers from the chromosome and plasmids of new hosts and store them permanently in their own array. Subsequent PCR amplification and sequencing of these expanded arrays provide a molecular record of both the bacterial hosts and the co-resident plasmids encountered. We created SPI plasmids using the backbones of well-characterized mobilizable and conjugative plasmids RSF1010, RP4, F, and R100-1. We tested SPI plasmids in defined laboratory matings and in complex wastewater communities. The analysis of the acquired spacers successfully mapped permissive host ranges and profiled the co-resident plasmids in situ. Requiring only standard cloning, PCR and sequencing, this accessible and cost-effective strategy establishes a new framework for studying plasmid ecology. Because spacers are integrated chronologically, it further offers the potential to reconstruct multi-step transfer trajectories across natural microbial networks.
